newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serb opposition plans "pet" protest in Belgrade.
newsitem.headline: Serb opposition plans "pet" protest in Belgrade.

text.p: Serbia's pro-democracy activists added a new twist to two months of daily demonstrations against autocratic President Slobodan Milosevic's government by urging supporters to take a pet for a walk in Belgrade on Sunday.
"They have banned our walks. They say the president thinks our walks are bad for our health," said Zoran Djindjic, a leader of the Zajedno (Together) opposition.
"But does our president like our dogs to walk? At 3 p.m. tomorrow, take out your dogs and let's see if they will be permitted to walk. And if you don't have a dog bring something else, maybe a duck."

Djindjic, who was due to meet German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel in Bonn on Sunday, was addressing 30,000 demonstrators who wore army fatigues, hospital garb, hockey kits and a motley array of other uniforms to a protest rally on Saturday.
His appeal came on the 62nd day of protests across Serbia to try to force Milosevic's government to accept that Zajedno candidates won control of 14 towns and cities in November elections.

Milosevic and his Socialist Party have so far resisted international pressure to recognise the results. Hardline Socialists say they will challenge electoral commission rulings acknowledging Zajedno's victory in Belgrade.

Speakers at a rally of thousands of Serbs on Saturday in ethnically-sensitive Kosovo province said ethnic Albanians, with support from the Serbian opposition, were responsible for a bomb attack on a university adminstrator.
Radivoye Papovic, rector of the University of Pristina, was critically wounded on Thursday when a bomb planted in a parked car exploded as his car passed by, local authorities said.
Private BK television quoted doctors at a Belgrade hospital, where Papovic was being treated, as saying that he would be out of intensive care on Monday.
The Serbian government revoked Kosovo's regional autonomy in 1989, accusing the 90 percent ethnic Albanian majority of wanting to secede and join Albania.
Pristina's Mayor Dusan Simic blamed the opposition and Albanian separatists for the bombing, telling the rally it showed "that Albanian extremists are ready to use the darkest methods..."

"Simic said Albanian extremists and separatists, who before the international community act as peacemakers, democrats and opposition demonstrators in Serbia stand here behind the darkest political terrorism and ethnic cleansing," the state-run Tanjug news agency reported.
In Belgrade, Zajedno released a statement condemning the bomb attack and denying the opposition was connected to it.
"Whoever committed this shameless action committed it against the democratisation of Serbia and against the interests of all citizens of Serbia," it said.
